content.title: About
content.content: Almonds are the edible seeds of the almond tree (Prunus dulcis), which is native to the Middle East and Central Asia and is now grown in many warm regions of the world. They have a mild, slightly sweet, nutty flavor and a crunchy texture. Almonds are eaten raw, roasted, or blanched and are used in baking, desserts, spreads, and almond milk.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Almonds are related to peaches, plums, and cherries, and the almond itself is the seed inside the fruit's pit.
Sweet almonds are the ones eaten as food; bitter almonds contain compounds that are toxic when raw and are not sold as ordinary snacks.
Almond trees have been cultivated for thousands of years.
Almonds are used to make almond flour, almond butter, marzipan, and almond milk.
Almond blossoms appear in early spring, before the leaves.

items.title: Rich in vitamin E
items.content: Almonds are one of the best food sources of vitamin E, an antioxidant that helps protect cells.

items.title: Provides healthy fats
items.content: Almonds contain mostly monounsaturated fats, which can be part of a heart-friendly diet.

items.title: Contains magnesium
items.content: Magnesium supports normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Provides protein and fiber
items.content: Almonds contribute plant protein and fiber, which support fullness.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Almonds contain more calcium than most other nuts.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Almonds can cause allergic reactions, which may be severe in some people.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Almonds are calorie-dense, so portions should be moderate.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Whole almonds are not suitable for young children because they can cause choking.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Almonds contain oxalates, which people prone to kidney stones may need to limit. Bitter almonds should never be eaten raw.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Almonds can be eaten as a snack, added to oatmeal, yogurt, salads, and baked goods, or ground into almond flour and almond butter. Soaking or blanching almonds softens them and makes the skins easy to remove. Unsalted or lightly salted almonds are a good option.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store almonds in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer storage, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer, since their oils can turn rancid. Discard almonds that smell bitter, sharp, or stale.

beef-steak-strip-lean-only-eaten.title: Beef, steak, strip, lean only eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Beef strip steak is a lean cut taken from the short loin of the cow. It contains very little fat, is rich in protein and essential micronutrients, and is commonly grilled, pan‑seared or oven‑roasted as thin slices.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The strip (also called New York strip) is one of the most tender beef cuts after filet mignon.
Lean strip steaks are popular in diet plans because they provide fewer calories than fattier cuts.
Beef is a natural source of creatine, which supports muscle energy metabolism.
In the United States the strip is a staple of steak‑house menus; in Japan it is sometimes served as a lightly seared sashimi‑style steak.
Beef contains more heme iron than most plant foods, making it an excellent source of absorbable iron.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Strip steak provides about 26 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Heme iron from beef is readily absorbed, helping maintain healthy hemoglobin levels.

items.title: Source of zinc
items.content: Zinc contributes to immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: A lean strip steak contains roughly 5 g of fat per 100 g, suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef supplies vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked beef may harbor harmful bacteria (E. coli, Salmonella). Cook to an internal temperature of at least 63 °C (145 °F).

items.title: High purine content
items.content: People with gout should limit intake of purine‑rich meats.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Rare, but some individuals can be allergic to beef.

items.title: Sodium in processed cuts
items.content: If the steak is pre‑marinated, watch the added salt.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook the strip steak on high heat for 2–3 minutes per side to the desired doneness. Slice thinly against the grain for salads, sandwiches, or Asian‑style dishes such as stir‑fry or steak tataki.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh steak in the refrigerator at 0–2 °C, sealed in an airtight bag, for 3–5 days. For longer storage, freeze at –18 °C in a vacuum‑sealed package for up to 6 months. Thaw frozen steak in the fridge before cooking.

corn-frozen-cooked-no-added-fat.title: Corn, frozen, cooked, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Corn is the grain of the annual grass Zea mays. Frozen cooked corn with no added fat is a ready‑to‑eat product that retains most nutrients and its natural sweet flavor after quick blanching and flash‑freezing.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Corn is one of the most widely consumed cereal crops worldwide.
Freezing immediately after cooking preserves the bright yellow color and crisp texture.
Corn contains carotenoids, especially lutein and zeaxanthin, which are beneficial for eye health.
In the United States frozen corn kernels are a common microwave side dish.
Corn with no added fat fits well into low‑fat dietary patterns.

items.title: Rich in carbohydrates
items.content: Corn provides a quick source of energy through complex carbs, useful for active individuals.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports normal digestive function and promotes satiety.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: It supplies thiamin, niacin and folate, which are important for metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin help protect the eyes from age‑related changes.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The absence of added fat makes it suitable for low‑fat diet plans.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to corn proteins.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Corn can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid may reduce the absorption of certain minerals when consumed in large amounts.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the corn in the microwave or on a skillet, add it to salads, soups, stews, or serve as a side dish with meat or fish. It pairs well with herbs, spices, and a drizzle of olive oil.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen corn in an airtight bag at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. After thawing, use within 2–3 days and do not leave at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Egg roll with shrimp is a classic Asian snack made from a thin omelette wrapped around sautéed shrimp, vegetables, and sometimes noodles. The roll is served hot, crispy on the outside and tender inside, often accompanied by soy sauce or a sweet‑sour dipping sauce.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The egg roll originated in Chinese street food in the early 20th century and quickly spread to Japan and the United States.
The delicate omelette wrapper cooks in just a few seconds on a very hot pan.
Shrimp are usually marinated in soy sauce, ginger, and garlic before being added to the roll, enhancing their flavor.
Traditional rolls often include crunchy vegetables such as carrots, cabbage, and bean sprouts for textural contrast.
In some regions the roll is finished with a fragrant oil, like sesame or garlic oil.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Shrimp provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many fried snacks, an egg roll contains moderate fat, especially when cooked with minimal oil.

items.title: Source of omega‑3
items.content: Shrimp contain omega‑3 fatty acids that support heart health and reduce inflammation.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The roll supplies B12 and B6 vitamins, important for nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Shrimp are rich in selenium, zinc, and iron, which aid immune function and hemoglobin formation.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Shrimp are a common allergen; individuals with shellfish allergy should avoid this product.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Sauces and marinades can increase sodium levels, which may be a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Improper storage or undercooking of shrimp can lead to foodborne illness.

items.title: High calories when deep‑fried
items.content: If the roll is deep‑fried, its calorie count rises significantly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the roll hot, sliced into bite‑size pieces. Dip it in soy sauce, sweet‑sour sauce, or chili sauce. For a lighter version, steam the roll first and then briefly pan‑fry to achieve a golden crust.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Freshly prepared rolls are best eaten immediately. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Reheat gently in an oven or skillet to restore crispness before serving.
